paras: The attempted lynching of Merrick Woodworth was a threatened lynching at Pueblo, Colorado, on November 1, 1880, of a 50-year-old man accused of being found in bed with his daughter. Woodworth was reported to have narrowly escaped, and the episode is known only from a one-line telegram reprinted in four Western and Midwestern papers.

According to a Pueblo dispatch dated November 2, Woodworth, aged 50, "narrowly escaped lynching yesterday for being found in bed with his daughter." Three papers gave the daughter's age as 13, while the Eureka Daily Sentinel's text reads 18, likely a misprint or misreading. The reports do not say who threatened him, how many took part, where it happened or how he escaped, and none gives his race.
No report of an arrest, charge or trial of Woodworth, or of any action against those who sought to lynch him, appears in the coverage.

The Cheyenne Daily Leader printed the item first, on November 2, in a column of "Brief Telegrams," giving the name as "Herrick Woodworth." The Eureka Daily Sentinel ran the same telegram the next day under the headings "A Rascally Old Father" and "An Old Rascal," directing its judgment at the accused man rather than at the threatened lynching. The Pioche Weekly Record reprinted the dispatch without comment on November 6.

On the same day the Lexington Weekly Intelligencer in Missouri rewrote the story as a single sentence among political paragraphs on the 1880 election, describing Woodworth as "a citizen of Pueblo" and stating the accusation as "the offense of debauching his 13-year-old daughter." None of the papers questioned the accusation or criticized the attempt at lynching.
